questions.q: What does this lesson's simulated disaster involve, specifically?
options: Total loss of the Columbus site — both SQLPRD01 and SQLPRD02 unreachable at once, leaving only the asynchronous SQLDR01 replica
A single disk failure on SQLPRD01 only
A planned, routine failover between SQLPRD01 and SQLPRD02
Loss of the backup files from Lesson 43, with all servers still running
questions.explain: This lesson tests the DR leg specifically — the scenario where the entire Columbus site, both local replicas, is gone at once.

questions.q: Why does SQL Server refuse a plain FAILOVER command in this scenario?
options: SQLDR01 is asynchronous and can't be confirmed as fully caught up once the other replicas that could confirm it are unreachable
FAILOVER only ever works when run from the primary replica
SQLDR01 has no failover capability at all
A plain FAILOVER would work fine and is what should be used here
questions.explain: Because asynchronous commit doesn't guarantee the secondary is caught up, and the replicas that could confirm it are gone, SQL Server requires the explicit FORCE_FAILOVER_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS acknowledgment instead.

options: It explicitly promotes an asynchronous replica to primary while acknowledging that some committed data may not have made it there
It forces a backup to run immediately before any failover
It permanently disables the failed replicas from ever rejoining
It is used for routine, planned failovers between synchronous replicas
questions.explain: This command is reserved specifically for promoting a replica when data loss can't be ruled out — exactly the case with an unreachable primary and an async secondary.

questions.q: Why does Bellhaven's runbook call for measuring the actual data-loss window instead of assuming it matched the 5-minute RPO?
options: The real gap depends on what was actually in flight when the site went down, and it must be verified, not assumed, before declaring the test successful
The RPO number is only a marketing figure with no operational meaning
SQL Server automatically reports the exact RPO after every forced failover
Measuring the gap is unnecessary once FORCE_FAILOVER_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS succeeds
questions.explain: A forced failover's actual data loss depends on real conditions at the time — it must be measured against timestamps, not assumed to equal the target RPO.

questions.q: What has to happen to SQLPRD01 and SQLPRD02 once the Columbus site is restored after this kind of disaster?
options: They rejoin AG_Bellhaven as new secondaries from scratch — the forced failover broke the original quorum relationship, so they don't automatically resume their old roles
They automatically resume as primary and synchronous secondary the moment power is restored
They can never rejoin the same Availability Group again
Nothing — the AG configuration is unaffected by a forced failover
questions.explain: A forced failover breaks the original relationship; recovering replicas have to rejoin and reseed as new secondaries under the promoted primary, SQLDR01.
